title: Generating Ideas
summary: Separate idea generation from judging, aim for quantity, use SCAMPER and constraints, and set idea quotas.
objectives: Explain divergent and convergent thinking and keep them apart.
Generate many ideas using SCAMPER and constraints.
Use an idea quota to push past obvious answers.

explanation.heading: Two kinds of thinking
explanation.body:
Creative work uses two modes. **Divergent thinking** opens up possibilities: many ideas, wild ones included, no judging. **Convergent thinking** narrows: compare, test and choose. Problems begin when both run together. If you criticise each idea as it appears, you stop after two or three safe ones. The rule is simple: generate first, judge later, and never in the same breath.

Schedule them separately. Spend ten minutes only producing ideas, then take a break, then spend ten minutes selecting. Even a small gap protects the first stage from your inner critic.

explanation.heading: Quantity first
explanation.body: The first ideas that come to mind are usually the obvious ones that everybody else has too. Better ideas often appear after the obvious ones are exhausted, so aim for **quantity**. Set a target, for example 20 ideas in 10 minutes, and keep writing when it feels empty. Write short phrases, not essays. Include silly or impossible ideas; they often contain a usable part. Do not edit while writing. If you are working in a group, let everyone write alone first, then share, so that loud voices do not steer the list.

explanation.heading: The SCAMPER method
explanation.body:
**SCAMPER** is a set of prompts for changing something that already exists. **S**ubstitute: what could replace a part? **C**ombine: what could be merged? **A**dapt: what can be borrowed from elsewhere? **M**odify: change size, shape or frequency. **P**ut to another use: who else could use this? **E**liminate: what can be removed? **R**earrange or reverse: change order or roles.

Apply it to a student attendance app: Combine attendance with timetable reminders; Eliminate manual roll calls by using a QR code; Put to another use: track lab equipment returns; Reverse: let students mark teachers' lateness. One familiar object, seven fresh directions.

explanation.heading: Constraints and quotas
explanation.body:
It seems odd, but limits improve creativity. A blank page offers too many options, while a constraint such as "design a study tool using only paper and no more than three steps" forces new thinking. Try limits on cost, time, materials or words.

An **idea quota** works the same way: "five ideas every morning before checking my phone". Over a month that is 150 ideas, and even a few useful ones change your work. Keep an idea list so that none are lost. Treat the quota as practice for the habit, not a test of quality. The more you practise producing, the less frightening an empty page becomes.

examples.title: SCAMPER on a notebook
examples.body: Substitute paper with a tablet; combine with a planner; adapt a ledger layout; modify to pocket size; put to another use as a bug log; eliminate lines; reverse so the back page is the index. Five minutes gave seven concepts, two of them new.
examples.takeaway: A framework gives you somewhere to start when your mind is blank.

examples.title: Constraint at work
examples.body: Asked to improve onboarding, Neha limits herself to "one page, no meeting". Ideas: a checklist, a welcome video, a buddy list. Without limits she had only suggested more meetings.
examples.takeaway: Constraints push you off the obvious path.

exercises.why: Divergent thinking opens possibilities without judging.

exercises.prompt: In SCAMPER, the letter E stands for ____. (one word)
exercises.why: E means eliminate: what can you remove?

exercises.prompt: Pick an everyday object (for example a water bottle or a to-do list app). Write at least six ideas using SCAMPER prompts, labelling each with its letter.
exercises.modelAnswer: Water bottle. S: substitute the cap with a filter. C: combine with a reminder light that glows each hour. A: adapt a cycling bottle clip for backpacks. M: make it collapsible. P: reuse as a desk pen holder. E: eliminate the label to save ink. R: reverse the flow so the bottle fills from the bottom.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers label each idea with its SCAMPER letter and include some unusual but plausible options. Avoid stopping after the first three.

exercises.prompt: In a group brainstorm someone says "That will never work" to your first idea. What helps most?

options.text: Suggest the group separate generating from judging and continue listing.

task.title: Ten-minute idea sprint
task.brief: Generate 20 ideas on a real problem and then choose three.
steps: Write the problem as a question.
Set a timer for ten minutes and list 20 ideas without judging.
Use two SCAMPER prompts if you get stuck.
After a break, mark your three best ideas and say why.
checklist: I did not judge while writing
I picked three and gave reasons
task.evidencePrompt: Write your problem and your three best ideas.

quiz.prompt: Judging every idea as it appears will:

options: Obvious ideas come first and better ones later
quiz.why: Better ideas appear after the obvious ones.
Combine is the C in SCAMPER.

quiz.prompt: A limit such as time or materials is called a ____. (one word)
quiz.why: Constraints focus thinking and push beyond the obvious.

bank.prompt: An idea quota of five a day builds:
bank.why: Regular practice builds the idea habit.
Rearrange or reverse changes order or roles.

cards.back: Divergent opens many options without judging; convergent narrows, compares and chooses.
Obvious ideas come first; better ones come after you push past them.
Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Rearrange/Reverse.
Limits remove the blank-page problem and force new routes.

reflection: When do you usually stop generating ideas too early, and what judging voice interrupts you?

keyPoints: Constraints and quotas build the habit.
revision.redo: Repeat the idea sprint on a different problem with a 25-idea target.
